The proposed h + σ(W[h;u]+b)⊙u is a context-conditioned gate on a residual update. Its core operation has substantial precedent: [GLUs](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/dauphin17a.html) multiply a linear feature branch by a sigmoid branch; [WaveNet](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.03499) uses tanh(Wf*x)⊙σ(Wg*x) inside causal dilated residual blocks; [TFT gated residual networks](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.09363v3) add a GLU-controlled transformation to an identity path, followed by normalization. Conditioning the gate explicitly on both h and u changes its parameterization, but does not establish a novel gating principle. The original [NextItNet paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.05163) introduces dilated convolutions and residual blocks, rather than this specific sigmoid residual-update gate.

These sources demonstrate predictive or optimization benefits, not suppression of stale recommendation interactions. GLU experiments support improved convergence/perplexity; WaveNet reports better audio modeling than ReLU; TFT’s gating ablation increases P90 loss by 1.9% on average. None establishes the proposed NextItNet mechanism. Algebraically, a small gate suppresses u while preserving h, including historical information already encoded there. When u mixes multiple history positions, its gate directly controls aggregated features; selective historical suppression remains a hypothesis.

Evidence needed: controlled validation interventions replacing stale or irrelevant interactions while preserving recent relevant history; comparison against constant gates and parameter-matched ungated blocks; reduced prediction sensitivity specifically to irrelevant history, while retaining useful older dependencies. Gate magnitudes or higher HR@10 alone cannot distinguish historical selection from feature rescaling, regularization, or easier optimization. Any claim should therefore remain “adaptive residual feature modulation” until interaction-specific interventions support the stronger mechanism.
